newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian doctors, nurses strike over unpaid wages.
newsitem.headline: Serbian doctors, nurses strike over unpaid wages.

text.p: Doctors and nurses will continue a strike over unpaid wages and neglect of the health sector after talks with the Serbian government produced no results, union officials said on Thursday.
The entire Clinical Centre in Belgrade, Serbia's biggest medical institution, is on strike, except for its emergency unit, they said.
"Some 75 percent of the 31,000 employed in all health care institutions in Serbia are on strike," Jasmina Kupresanin, an official of the Belgrade health workers trade union said.
On strike are health care institutions in Belgrade and 18 other towns, the union said.
All institutions were providing a minimum level of services, standard for weekends and holidays.
Strikers were demanding the payment of their March and April salaries, increases on last year's salaries, and the normalisation of payments by September.
"The government is short of hundreds of millions of dinars to meet our demands," trade union president Stevan Djordjevic said after meeting government officials.

The Yugoslav government is chronically strapped for cash after the National Bank refused to print money. Belgrade is barred from foreign funding by a U.S.-imposed "outer wall" of sanctions pending improvement of its human rights record.
The country's economy has not recovered from four years of crippling U.N. sanctions, mismanagement and wars in Croatia and Bosnia between 1992 and 1995.
Independent Belgrade media report that the government would need some 300 million dinars ($55 million) to meet the strikers' demands and normalise the situation in the health care sector.
The strikers accuse the Serbian government of gross mismanagement and neglect of the health care sector, which is also suffering shortages of medicines and equipment.

Big pharmaceutical companies in Serbia, including ICN Galenika, have delivered drugs worth up to $80 million for which they have not been paid by the state, Serbian health minister Leposava Milicevic said.
Most of the patients in hospitals have to provide their own medication, which in many cases costs more than they can afford.
"Just recently my colleague told me that during her night duty three patients were suffocating and she had only one Urbason to give," Kupresanin said. Urbason is a treatment for asthma.
The government has exempted from health care taxes major concerns such as the power company, iron and metal works, a trade union official said.
"(Serbian Prime Minister) Mirko Marjanovic must publicly come out and say whether Serbia needs its health care service or do we have to revert to spells and witchcraft," he said.
